section_summary: This section consists of clippings from the English-language press in Tokyo (primarily The Japan Advertiser, including translations of editorials from the Fukuoka Nichi-Nichi, Tokyo Nichi-Nichi, and Hochi) covering Japanese Diet sessions, political commentary, and official reports between January 31 and February 4, 1934. Parliamentary interpellations focus heavily on foreign affairs—including the Indo-Japanese trade pact, Soviet-Japanese border and fishery disputes, relations with the United States and Great Britain, and upcoming naval ratio negotiations—alongside sharp debates over military interference in civilian governance and the administrative status of Manchukuo. The materials also detail domestic political party maneuvers against the non-party Saito Cabinet, legislative stagnation, industrial controversies surrounding the Japan Iron Foundry merger and Teikoku Rayon stock transactions, and official government statistics on salaries, banking, foreign currency assets, and ministerial secret funds.

subfiles.about: A report on Lower House Budget Committee interpellations regarding the Indo-Japanese trade pact, Soviet-Manchukuo border defense, China policy, and environmental damage from the Ashio copper mine.
subfiles.summary: Clipping: Diet budget committee members denounce the Indo-Japanese trade outcome and press Hirota and Hayashi on the Soviet-Manchukuo frontier; Hirota proposes demilitarization and denies immediate danger.
subfiles.title: Indian Trade Pact Denounced in Diet as Blow to Japan

subfiles.about: An editorial calling upon the Ministry of Home Affairs to suppress militaristic publications and rightist movements with the same vigor applied to communist activities.
subfiles.from: Fukuoka Nichi Nichi / The Japan Advertiser
subfiles.summary: Fukuoka Nichi Nichi welcomes Home Ministry curbs on war-stimulating publications but reproaches it for tolerating chauvinist propaganda while suppressing communism, warning of hostility abroad and a threat to the Imperial system.
subfiles.title: Control Over Books

subfiles.about: A detailed report on Diet proceedings reviewing Soviet-Japanese relations, naval limitation treaties, South Seas mandates, northern fishery negotiations, and the Japan Iron Foundry merger.
subfiles.summary: Clipping: former Foreign Minister Yoshizawa argues Japan and the Soviet Union have no real cause for war; Hirota says the South Seas mandate is unaffected; the Japan Iron Foundry merger and farm relief are debated.
subfiles.title: Diet Speaker Says Russia, Japan Have No Real War Cause

subfiles.about: An official statistical release by the Navy Ministry comparing Japanese and American naval strength and treaty ratios projected to the end of 1936.
subfiles.summary: Navy Ministry tables project end-1936 fleets at 0.68 to 1.00 favoring the U.S. counting over-age ships, but 0.81 to 1.00 favoring Japan within treaty age limits, per Osumi.
subfiles.title: Naval Comparisons of U. S., Japan Given

subfiles.about: A report on Diet sessions questioning cabinet ministers over military political interference, defense reorganization, air force unification, and national expenditures.
subfiles.summary: Clipping: Diet members criticize military political activism and foreign policy after Japan's League withdrawal; Saito and Hayashi reject a unified defense ministry; Hikita protests public adulation of Hara's assassin Nakaoka.
subfiles.title: Questioning in Diet Criticizes Defense and Foreign Policy

subfiles.about: A brief news item reporting Lower House member Eikichi Hikita's disclosure that retired generals had approached Premier Saito demanding his resignation.
subfiles.summary: Seiyukai member Hikita says retired generals urged Premier Saito to resign, warning that military political pronouncements and Meirinkai attacks on parties alienate the army from civilians.
subfiles.title: Diet Speaker Claims Saito Asked to Quit By Retired Generals

subfiles.about: An analytical article by Dr. S. Washio examining the political parties' coordinated parliamentary offensive against the military and the non-party Saito Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Dr. Washio: Seiyukai and Minseito formed a united front against military dominance, then backed off for fear of backlash and turned to Commerce Minister Nakajima's scandals, yielding few results.
subfiles.title: Diet Attack Against Military Aims at Restoring Party Rule

subfiles.about: An editorial examining why foreign powers, particularly the Soviet Union, have received Foreign Minister Hirota's cooperative diplomatic overtures with skepticism.
subfiles.summary: Hochi notes Britain and the U.S. cautiously favored Hirota's conciliatory Diet address while Soviet leaders distrusted it, and warns against accommodation with unseemly haste.
subfiles.title: Hirota Not Comprehended

subfiles.about: An editorial commending the constructive exchange between Kenkichi Yoshizawa and Foreign Minister Hirota in the House of Peers regarding diplomatic moderation.
subfiles.summary: Nichi-Nichi welcomes Yoshizawa's interpellation and Hirota's replies, backing naval ratio revision, diplomatic solutions with the Soviet Union, and calm over a supposed 1935-1936 crisis.
subfiles.title: Yoshizawa Encourages Hirota

subfiles.about: A report on Lower House interpellations demanding reform of the Kwantung Army's multiple administrative offices and criticizing military political encroachment.
subfiles.summary: Ikeda challenges the concentration of Manchurian offices in one general; Hayashi calls the system anomalous but indispensable and denies military dictatorship plans.
subfiles.title: Need of Clarifying Japan's Position in Manchuria Pressed

subfiles.about: An editorial asserting Japan's right to demand naval armament equality and an upward revision of treaty ratios at the 1935 conference.
subfiles.summary: Nichi-Nichi argues Japan must insist on equality in defensive armaments at the 1935 naval parley, calling Washington Treaty ratios a temporary expedient.
subfiles.title: Japan to Ask Equality

subfiles.about: An editorial commending the Diet for restoring its public stature by addressing national issues with sobriety and dampening alarmism over an impending crisis.
subfiles.summary: Hochi praises the Diet's constructive questioning, dispelling fatalism about a 1935-1936 crisis, but cautions against premature impeachment over Nakajima's iron foundry merger.
subfiles.title: Diet Politics Picking Up

subfiles.about: An official compilation of government statistical reports submitted to the Diet budget committee detailing secret funds, official salaries, foreign securities, and bank deposits.
subfiles.summary: Government statistics to the Diet: 1931-1932 official salaries of 169,058,000 yen, 1934-1935 secret funds of 13,814,800 yen (War Ministry 7,334,405), and banking deposits of 10.55 billion yen.
subfiles.title: Government Gives Statistics to Diet

subfiles.about: A report on a statement by the Kokumin Domei condemning the Saito Government and majority parties for delaying essential agrarian and election reform legislation.
subfiles.summary: Kokumin Domei leaders draft a declaration criticizing the Saito Cabinet and the Seiyukai and Minseito for failing to submit farm relief and election law reforms; Matsutani will speak on the Peace Preservation Law.
subfiles.title: Ministry Criticized by Kokumin Domei
